title: Wax on Sand
passage:
At half past six the indoor school is lit, empty and cold, and the tractor is already in it, towing a leveller the width of a small car down the long side. What it is levelling is not soil. The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand, mixed through with chopped synthetic fibre and coated in wax, laid over a membrane and a bed of crushed stone. It went down nine years ago. For two winters the riders here have been saying that the school changes under them – hard and slippery for the first lesson of a January morning, deep and tiring by the end of a July afternoon – and the yard has had three explanations to pick from: the machine, the mix, or the man on the tractor.

Mervyn Pallenhurst tests riding surfaces for an insurer that covers about four hundred schools and yards. He came in February with a drop tester in the back of the car: a steel foot on a rail, weighted to something near what a forelimb puts down, released from a fixed height, with an accelerometer bolted inside it. It reports two numbers – how sharply the surface stops the foot, and how far the foot slides before it stops. He took a grid of readings at seven in the morning, with the school at three degrees, and the same grid at four in the afternoon, with it at eighteen. Both numbers moved, and they moved together: in the cold the foot stopped in about two-thirds of the distance it needed in the warm, and it slid less doing it. He has been back four times since, in July as well as in January. He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas. In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another. The waxed ones move. “The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is,” Pallenhurst says. “I wouldn’t put a crossover figure on it yet – two winters of readings is not enough for that – but the gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test.”

The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing the whole of that. Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together, and a hoof breaks the surface rather than pushing it aside; between eight and twenty the wax is tacky enough to hold the sand loosely and soft enough to let it move; above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep. A waxed floor is never watered, which is half of why yards buy one. Then there is the machine, though not in the way the yard meant it. The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. The bed is 130. Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on. Pallenhurst cored the bed in eleven places. In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3. Harrowing lifts fibre, and fibre is what keeps sand from packing, so the machine had been quietly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one. The sand itself had hardly changed: the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them, and the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.

What the yard wants to know, and what riders everywhere want to know, is whether any of it keeps a horse sound. Here Pallenhurst is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him. The tester measures a surface. There is no horse above his steel foot and no leg to take what comes back up it. He has readings from a hundred and forty arenas and injury records he would trust from hardly any of them, because the yards that keep good records are the yards that do everything else well, and the comparison is spoilt before it starts. The one association he will argue for is not with any surface but with change – a horse schooled on one footing and jumped on another – and he says he would argue it from the veterinary literature rather than from his own figures. That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are.

The yard has changed two things and left the rest alone. A timer brings the heaters on at five, to have the school above eight degrees before the first lesson; the bill is real and the yard has decided it is worth paying. The tines have been dropped to 80 millimetres, with a length of angle iron welded across the frame so that nobody has to set them by eye, and for the first month the tractor went over the school twice a day to bring the pan up. At ten past seven on a February morning the tine marks run the length of the school in even rows, and the thermometer screwed to the post by the gate reads nine.
– Bridget Tozer

questions.prompt: What is said about the readings Pallenhurst took inside the school?

options.text: The two numbers his tester reports moved in opposite directions between the morning and the afternoon.
The foot was let go from a lower point in the cold, and stopped sooner for it.
In the cold the same drop stopped the foot in a shorter distance and slid less.
He read the school at the two ends of one February day and has not been back.

questions.prompt: What was shown by the cores Pallenhurst took from the bed?

options.text: The wax had worn off the grains in the lower part of the bed.
The sand had broken down into finer grains than the specification called for.
Below the tines the bed had stayed loose, since no hoof reaches that deep.
There was much less fibre in the bottom of the bed than in the top.

questions.prompt: What is suggested about the schools Pallenhurst tests that are kept damp rather than waxed?

options.text: Their beds are newer, so the wax in them has not begun to wear.
Having no wax in them is what leaves them riding much the same all day.
They carry no fibre, so there is nothing in them to stiffen when the school is cold.
They are read at a different hour, so the two grids never catch the change.

questions.prompt: How does the writer regard the idea that testing of this kind can show which arenas keep horses sound?

options.text: She takes the limits Pallenhurst sets on his own figures to be the honest ones.
She treats the tie between changing a horse’s footing and injury as settled by his readings.
She thinks work of this kind gives a yard nothing it can act on.
She thinks the riders’ complaints were the part of the story worth doubting.

questions.prompt: What can be concluded from this text?

options.text: The cold is probably doing damage to a bed that is near the end of its life.
A school that is kept warm will ride in February much as it rides in July.
The school’s temperature and the depth the tines reach are what settle how it rides.
The tractor’s work may matter more to the school than the temperature does.
